name: Japan
traditionNote: A codified civil-law system built on six principal codes, so the starting point is almost always the consolidated statute text rather than a line of cases; court decisions are highly persuasive but are not formally binding precedent.
summary: The National Diet (国会), made up of the House of Representatives and the House of Councillors, enacts statutes (法律); the Cabinet issues Cabinet orders (政令) and ministries issue ministerial ordinances (省令). Everything is promulgated in the Kanpō (官報), the official gazette, published every business day. Since 1 April 2025, under the Act on the Issuance of Official Gazettes (Act No. 85 of 2023), the Kanpō is issued by being posted on the government's gazette site and the electronic data there — carrying an electronic signature and timestamp — is the authentic original (正本); the printed edition is no longer the version of record. The authentic text exists only in Japanese; the government's English translations are explicitly reference material with no legal effect. Statutes take effect on the date specified in the act itself or in the accompanying enforcement order, which is often later than promulgation.
hierarchy: Cabinet Office and ministerial ordinances (内閣府令・省令)
Agency rules and public notices (規則・告示)

gazette.name: Kanpo
gazette.authority: Cabinet Office, Minister's Secretariat General Affairs Division (内閣府大臣官房総務課)
gazette.coverage: Current issues every business day from 08:30; free full view for roughly 90 days; PDFs of laws and Cabinet orders from the former internet edition back to 15 July 2003, and government-procurement notices back to 1 April 2016
gazette.desc: The gazette of record: every statute, Cabinet order, ministerial ordinance, treaty, public notice and appointment is promulgated here. Since 1 April 2025 the site itself is the act of publication and the signed electronic data on it is the authentic original of the Kanpō.
gazette.howto: The front page is a dated list, not a calendar: 本日の官報 shows today's issue and 直近90日間の官報 lists the last 90 days, most recent first. Each date row links to that day's 本紙 (main), 号外 (extra), 政府調達 (procurement) and, when issued, 特別号外, each in HTML and PDF, plus a full-contents view. Anything older sits under 過去の官報 (https://www.kanpo.go.jp/old/), which opens on the most recent archived month and is browsed by year and month. Check the embedded electronic certificate and timestamp on the PDF to confirm the copy is unaltered.
gazette.note: The old National Printing Bureau site kanpou.npb.go.jp closed on 31 March 2025; links to it are dead. There is no free keyword search of the full historical run on this site — see the paid Kanpō Information Search Service.

constitution.name: Nihonkoku Kenpo (e-Gov)
constitution.authority: Digital Agency (デジタル庁), e-Gov Law Search
constitution.coverage: Promulgated 3 November 1946 (昭和二十一年憲法), in force 3 May 1947; never amended
constitution.desc: The Japanese text of the Constitution inside the government's own consolidated law database — preamble plus 103 articles in eleven chapters. This is the version other government systems point at, identified by the law ID 321CONSTITUTION.
constitution.howto: Open the URL directly, or search 日本国憲法 from the e-Gov Law Search front page. The same text is retrievable as XML from the legacy API at https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/api/1/lawdata/321CONSTITUTION, or as JSON from the current version 2 API at https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/api/2/law_data/321CONSTITUTION; both return law ID 321CONSTITUTION with promulgation date 1946-11-03.
constitution.note: The Constitution has not been amended since it came into force in 1947, so there is no consolidation problem here — but the authentic text is the Japanese one only.

sources.name: e-Gov Horei Kensaku
sources.authority: Digital Agency (デジタル庁); formerly Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications
sources.coverage: Roughly 9,500 instruments in force — Constitution, Acts, Cabinet orders, Cabinet Office and ministerial ordinances, agency rules — kept as amended; the version 2 API reported 9,541 in August 2026, the oldest being a Dajokan proclamation of 1872
sources.desc: The government's consolidated database of law currently in force, fed from the e-LAWS drafting system. This, not the gazette, is where you read the current text of a statute; the gazette gives you the amending instrument, e-Gov gives you the result.
sources.howto: Use the keyword box for the law name, or browse by 法令種別 (Act / Cabinet order / ministerial ordinance) and by subject category. Each law page carries its law number, promulgation date and a version selector for past and not-yet-effective consolidations; https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/update/ lists recently updated instruments with their enforcement dates, and https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/bulkdownload/ offers the whole corpus as XML.
sources.note: Site moved from elaws.e-gov.go.jp to laws.e-gov.go.jp; old links redirect. It carries laws in force, not repealed historic text.

sources.name: Kanpo Joho Kensaku Service
sources.native: 官報情報検索サービス
sources.authority: National Printing Bureau (独立行政法人国立印刷局), under approval of the Prime Minister
sources.coverage: 3 May 1947 (the day the Constitution took effect) to the latest issue
sources.desc: The only comprehensive keyword search of the gazette back to 1947. The free gazette site gives you roughly 90 days plus date-by-date PDFs from 2003; this is what you use when you have to find a promulgation and do not know its date.
sources.howto: Subscribe (a membership account, ¥2,200 per month including tax, as of April 2025), then search by date, by keyword, or by ministry name and issue number for laws, Cabinet orders and treaties.
sources.note: Paid membership required. Service description page: https://search.npb.go.jp/guide/introduce.html

sources.name: Nihon Horei Sakuin
sources.en: Index of Japanese Laws and Regulations
sources.authority: National Diet Library (国立国会図書館)
sources.coverage: Laws from February 1886 (Meiji 19) onward, with their enactment, amendment and repeal history; ordinances and directives in force as of August 2004 onward; a separate Early Meiji edition (明治前期編) covers October 1868 to February 1888
sources.desc: The legislative-history index. It answers what a law was called, what number it had, what amended it, when it was repealed, and how the bill moved through the Imperial Diet or the Diet — the questions e-Gov cannot answer because it only carries law in force.
sources.howto: Search by law title, law number or Diet session under 法令沿革 to trace an instrument's history, or under 制定法律 / 審議情報 to find the bill and its Diet proceedings. Entries link out to full text where available.
sources.note: This is an index of legislative metadata and history, not a full-text statute database.

sources.name: Saibanrei Kensaku
sources.authority: Supreme Court of Japan (最高裁判所)
sources.coverage: Supreme Court, High Courts, lower-court express reports (from March 2002), and administrative, labour and intellectual-property case collections; lower-court administrative cases from the 1960s to 1997 plus selected later cases
sources.desc: The judiciary's own free case database, split into six collections. This is the official source for the text of Japanese judgments; commercial databases are broader but this one is authoritative and free.
sources.howto: Choose a collection, then search by case number (era, year, symbol, number), by decision date or range, by referenced statute, or by full text / holding keywords with AND-OR operators.
sources.note: The site states plainly that not all decisions are included (本裁判例情報には、すべての判決等が掲載されているわけではありません) — it is a selection, not a complete reporter. The older /app/hanrei_jp/search1 address still redirects here.

sources.name: Japanese Law Translation
sources.native: 日本法令外国語訳データベースシステム
sources.coverage: Selected statutes, Cabinet orders and ministerial ordinances in English; a mix of finalised and tentative translations
sources.desc: The government's own English translations, with Japanese-English parallel display and a standard legal-terms dictionary. The best English starting point precisely because it tells you where it is only tentative.
sources.howto: Use Law Search by title or keyword, then pick the /en (English), /ja (Japanese) or /je (bilingual) view; Dictionary Search and Keyword-in-Context Search handle terminology. Each law page offers downloads as plain text (.txt), PDF, Word (.docx) and a .tmx translation-memory file.
sources.note: The site states that translations are not official texts and that only the original Japanese has legal effect; some entries are marked tentative and unproofread.

sources.name: Shugiin gian joho
sources.en: House of Representatives — bills and legislative measures
sources.coverage: Bills, budgets, treaties and resolutions by Diet session, with full texts and progress records; the session index reaches back to the 142nd Diet (1998) and forward to the 221st
sources.desc: The lower house's bill register: as-introduced texts and the passage record for Cabinet bills, member bills and committee bills. Where you go for the text of something that has not been promulgated yet.
sources.howto: This URL always opens the current Diet session only (the 221st as of August 2026), listing bills by originating chamber with a 本文 link for the text and a 経過 link for the progress record. There is no session picker on it — for any other session go to the 国会回次一覧 index at https://www.shugiin.go.jp/internet/itdb_gian.nsf/html/gian/menu_all.htm, which lists the 142nd Diet onward.
sources.note: Bill text here is as introduced; committee amendments mean the enacted text can differ. Check the Kanpō for what was actually promulgated. Pages are served in Shift_JIS, which trips up some scrapers.

sources.name: Sangiin gian joho
sources.coverage: Bills, budgets, treaties, personnel consents and resolutions by Diet session; the session selector reaches back to the 153rd Diet
sources.desc: The upper house's counterpart register, with bill summaries (議案要旨) alongside the submitted texts — the summaries are often the fastest way to understand what a bill actually does.
sources.howto: Use the 国会回次指定 dropdown at the top of the page to move between Diet sessions — it lists every session from the 153rd to the current one — then open a bill for its 議案要旨 summary and PDF text.
sources.note: The URL is session-numbered and there is no stable session-agnostic index, so this link points at the 221st Diet (特別会, 18 February to 25 July 2026), the most recent as of August 2026; the dropdown on the page is the way to reach other sessions.

sources.name: Kokkai Kaigiroku Kensaku System
sources.native: 国会会議録検索システム
sources.authority: National Diet Library (国立国会図書館) with both houses of the Diet
sources.coverage: Plenary and committee proceedings from the 1st Diet session (1947) onward, in text and page-image form
sources.desc: Full-text searchable Diet proceedings. This is where the legislative intent behind a provision lives — minister and bureau-chief answers in committee are the standard material for arguing what a statute means.
sources.howto: Search by keyword, speaker, house, committee name and date range; each hit links to the meeting record and the page image. A documented API returns XML or JSON.

sources.name: Naikaku Hoseikyoku - saikin no horitsu joyaku
sources.native: 内閣法制局 最近の法律・条約
sources.en: Cabinet Legislation Bureau — recent laws and treaties
sources.coverage: Cabinet-submitted bill and treaty lists by Diet session back to the 206th Diet; lists of promulgated laws by year back to Heisei 30 (2018)
sources.desc: The clean official tally of what the Cabinet put before the Diet and what actually became law each year. Faster than either chamber's site when the question is simply 'which acts were promulgated in this year'.
sources.howto: Open 内閣提出法律案一覧 for a given Diet session to see bills and their fate, or 公布法律一覧 for a calendar year to see promulgated acts with their law numbers and promulgation dates.

sources.name: e-Gov Public Comment
sources.native: e-Govパブリック・コメント
sources.en: e-Gov public comment (notice and comment) portal
sources.authority: Digital Agency (デジタル庁) / e-Gov, for all national administrative organs
sources.coverage: Draft Cabinet orders, ministerial ordinances and other 命令等 open for comment, plus closed cases with the agency's response to submitted opinions
sources.desc: The single national portal for the statutory notice-and-comment procedure (意見公募手続). Drafts of subordinate legislation appear here before they exist anywhere else, together with the reasoning agencies give when they publish the final version.
sources.howto: Browse 案件一覧 filtered by status — currently open, closed, or results published — and by ministry. A results entry shows the draft, the comments received and the agency's reply.
sources.note: Comment periods are normally at least 30 days; a draft here is a proposal only and has no legal effect until promulgated in the Kanpō.

sources.name: Joyaku Data Kensaku
sources.coverage: Treaties in force approved by the Diet, drawn from the Kanpō and the ministry's annual treaty collection (条約集)
sources.desc: The searchable register of Japan's treaties, linking through to scanned images from the official treaty collection. Treaties are promulgated in the Kanpō like statutes, but this is where they are indexed as a set.
sources.howto: Search by treaty name, by subject classification, or by region and country; results display the page images from the 条約集. For treaties submitted to the Diet from the 154th session (2002) onward, the ministry's own treaty pages under https://www.mofa.go.jp/mofaj/gaiko/treaty/ carry the text, the approval history and the explanatory material.
sources.note: The whole mofa.go.jp estate sits behind an Akamai filter that returns 403 Access Denied to automated clients, so this link must be opened in an ordinary browser. The database itself is live — the National Diet Library's treaty research guide cites this exact address as the register of Diet-approved treaties in force.

sources.name: Kokuritsu Kokkai Toshokan Digital Collections
sources.native: 国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション
sources.authority: National Diet Library (国立国会図書館)
sources.coverage: Digitised Kanpō from the first issue of 2 July 1883 to 30 April 1952, including extras and the digitised monthly indexes, plus the English-edition OFFICIAL GAZETTE published from 4 April 1946 to 28 April 1952, the eve of the San Francisco Peace Treaty taking effect
sources.desc: The historical gazette. For anything promulgated before May 1952 this is the free full-run archive; the paid Kanpō search service starts only at 1947 and the free gazette site only at 2003.
sources.howto: Search the collection for 官報 and filter by date, or browse the digitised newspaper category; issues are page images with OCR-assisted search.
sources.note: Page images of the printed gazette — quality and OCR vary, and pre-1952 issues are in historical orthography.

sources.name: Tokyo-to Reikishu Database
sources.native: 東京都例規集データベース
sources.authority: Tokyo Metropolitan Government, General Affairs Bureau, Documents Division (東京都総務局総務部文書課)
sources.coverage: All ordinances (条例) and regulations (規則) of the Tokyo Metropolitan Government plus directives (訓令) and public notices (告示), digitised from the fifteen-volume printed 東京都令規集 and consolidated to a stated cut-off date — 15 June 2026 when checked in August 2026
sources.desc: A representative prefectural 例規集. Every prefecture and almost every municipality runs one of these, most of them on the same Reiki-Base platform, and it is the only place a local ordinance's current text is published online.
sources.howto: Click 利用を開始する to enter, then use 体系検索 to browse the subject tree (福祉, 都市整備 and so on), 五十音検索 to browse by the reading of the instrument's title, or the keyword box. Titles beginning 東京都 are filed under the reading of the word that follows.
sources.note: Consolidated to a cut-off date and not instantaneous — the site warns that ordinances and regulations carried in the 東京都公報 after that date are not yet reflected. The interface is only tested on Edge and Chrome.

sources.name: Research Navi - Nihon no horei
sources.native: リサーチ・ナビ 日本の法令
sources.en: NDL Research Navi — Japanese law research guides
sources.authority: National Diet Library (国立国会図書館)
sources.coverage: Around nineteen research guides covering gazette research, early Meiji and former-colonial law, ordinances, treaties, registration precedents and English translations
sources.desc: The librarian's map of the whole system, written by the National Diet Library. Worth reading first when the instrument you need is old, local, or from a period whose publication rules were different.
sources.howto: Pick the guide matching your problem — 日本-官報（法令情報）の調べ方 for gazette research, 日本-条例の調べ方 for local ordinances, 日本-明治前期の法令の調べ方 for early modern law, 日本-条約の調べ方 for treaties — each lists the specific databases and printed sets to use, with their exact coverage dates.

sources.name: Westlaw Japan
sources.coverage: Statutes (法令), case law (判例), administrative and quasi-judicial decisions (審決等), books and journals, bibliographic data and news, marketed as a single 日本法総合オンラインサービス
sources.desc: One of the subscription databases Japanese practitioners actually work in. It matters because its case coverage and editorial headnotes go well beyond the judiciary's free selection, and it carries the administrative decisions that no free government source collects in one place.
sources.howto: Subscription access, usually through a firm or a university library; search statutes, cases and secondary literature from one interface. Free trials are offered, and add-on subscriptions (Westlaw LIBRARY, Westlaw BOOK PLUS) cover the book and journal content.
sources.note: Private and paywalled. Its statute and case texts are reproductions — the authentic text remains the Kanpō and the court's own judgment.

sources.name: Kanpo Kensaku!
sources.authority: Privately operated by an individual; no government affiliation
sources.coverage: Full-text index of internet-published Kanpō issues; the index had not advanced past the issue of 15 January 2026 when checked in August 2026
sources.desc: A free full-text keyword search over the gazette, run by a private individual. Included because the official free site has no keyword search at all and the official search service is paywalled.
sources.howto: Type a keyword — a company name, a law title, a person's name — into the search box and open the matching gazette page.
sources.note: Explicitly not official and not affiliated with the government or the National Printing Bureau; treat hits as pointers and verify against kanpo.go.jp. Updating is unreliable — the site carries a notice that it had stopped and was restored, and as of August 2026 it was roughly seven months behind the gazette, so it cannot be relied on for anything recent.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of a national statute
findLaw.steps: Search the law's Japanese title in the e-Gov Law Search keyword box, or browse by 法令種別 and subject category. The page shows the consolidated text as amended, with the law number and promulgation date in the header and a version selector for earlier or not-yet-effective consolidations.

findLaw.task: See what changed recently, and read the amendment as promulgated
findLaw.steps: Open the e-Gov 更新法令一覧 for the rolling list of updated instruments with their enforcement dates. To read the amending act itself in its promulgated form, find its date and open that day's issue on the official gazette site; for a promulgation whose date you do not know, use the paid Kanpō Information Search Service.
findLaw.source: e-Gov Horei Kensaku (e-Gov法令検索), with 官報 and 官報情報検索サービス

findLaw.steps: Go to the Supreme Court's 裁判例検索 and choose the right collection — Supreme Court, High Courts, lower-court express reports, or the administrative, labour and IP collections. Search by case number, decision date range, cited statute, or full-text keyword. Not every judgment is included, so a subscription database may be needed for unreported decisions.
findLaw.source: Saibanrei Kensaku (裁判例検索), Courts in Japan

findLaw.task: Find subordinate legislation — Cabinet orders, ministerial ordinances, notices
findLaw.steps: Cabinet orders (政令) and ministerial ordinances (省令) are in the same e-Gov database as statutes; filter by 法令種別 to narrow to them. For instruments still in draft, and for the agency's published response to comments, check the e-Gov public comment portal. Public notices (告示) that are not carried in e-Gov appear in the Kanpō.
findLaw.source: e-Gov法令検索 and e-Govパブリック・コメント

findLaw.task: Find a prefectural or municipal ordinance
findLaw.steps: Go to the relevant local government's own 例規集 database — Tokyo's is a good model of the format, and most prefectures and cities run the same Reiki-Base style system. Browse the systematic table of contents or search by ordinance name and number; check the stated consolidation date at the top.
findLaw.source: Tokyo-to Reikishu Database (東京都例規集データベース)

findLaw.task: Trace a law's history, or find the bill and the debate behind it
findLaw.steps: Use the National Diet Library's 日本法令索引 to trace enactment, amendment and repeal back to 1886 and to identify the bill. Then open the bill text and progress record on the House of Representatives or House of Councillors bill pages, and search the committee record in the Diet Proceedings Search System for the ministerial explanations.
findLaw.source: 日本法令索引, 衆議院/参議院 議案, 国会会議録検索システム

findLaw.task: Read a Japanese law in English
findLaw.steps: Search the law title in the Japanese Law Translation database run by the Ministry of Justice and open the /en or bilingual /je view. Check whether the entry is marked tentative, and treat the Japanese column as the operative text in any case.
findLaw.source: Japanese Law Translation (日本法令外国語訳データベースシステム)

subnational: Japan is a unitary state, but prefectures and municipalities have genuine legislative power: under the Constitution and the Local Autonomy Act they enact ordinances (条例) and regulations (規則) within the limits of national law. Each local government promulgates these in its own gazette (公報) and publishes a consolidated 例規集 database on its website — Tokyo's is at reiki.metro.tokyo.lg.jp, and most others use the same Reiki-Base style platform. There is no single national database of local ordinances on the government side; you must go to the specific prefecture, city, town or village, and practitioners who need to search ordinances across jurisdictions fall back on commercial databases. Note that these 例規集 are consolidated only to a stated cut-off date — Tokyo's stood at 15 June 2026 in August 2026 — so anything carried in the local 公報 since then will not yet be reflected.
caveats: The authentic text is the Japanese text: since 1 April 2025 the authentic original of the Kanpō is the signed electronic data on kanpo.go.jp, and before that it was the printed edition — the English translations on the Ministry of Justice site are explicitly not official and have no legal effect, and many are marked tentative. e-Gov Law Search gives you consolidated text as amended, which is convenient but is not the as-promulgated instrument; when the exact wording matters, go back to the gazette issue. Free access to the gazette is thin: the current site gives roughly 90 days plus date-by-date PDFs from July 2003, keyword search back to 1947 is behind a ¥2,200-per-month subscription, and the pre-1952 run sits separately in NDL Digital Collections. The old gazette site kanpou.npb.go.jp closed on 31 March 2025, so older citations and links to it are dead. The judiciary's free case search is a curated selection and states so — absence of a judgment there does not mean it does not exist — and kanpoo.jp, despite its subject matter, is a private site with no government affiliation.
